extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of Restoration drama (Dryden and contemporaries); editors and literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical remarks for assessing Restoration-era comedies (production, authorship, and reception), drawn from an editor's commentary and prologue/epilogue material on Dryden's The Assignation. Focuses on dramatic action, title, taste, originality, performance, and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lameness of the action
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak, ill-constructed or 'lame' dramatic action can cause a play's failure regardless of other merits; the author himself hints at 'the lameness of the action' as a possible ground for the poor reception. When action is defective, blame is often shuffled between poet and performers, but the structural vitality of the plot is decisive for success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title sensitivity / provocative subtitle
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's second title, e.g. 'Love in a Nunnery,' may predispose audiences to hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A title or subtitle that suggests irreligion or scandal can provoke suspicions (here: that the author intends to ridicule the Duke of York or the Catholic religion) and lead enemies to condemn the piece before seeing it; choose titles mindful of contemporary political and religious sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridiculing powerful persons or religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that a play 'could... have been justly suspected of an intention to ridicule the Duke of York and the Catholic religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that appears to attack or mock prominent individuals or established religion risks inflaming audience hostility and bringing political/religious censure; tread carefully in satire aimed at powerful institutions or figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey morals by example, not dull moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not with dull morals, gravely writ, like those...but by examples drawn"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction in comedy should come through enacted examples and entertaining depiction rather than heavy-handed, didactic moralizing; audience prefer lively illustration of vice and virtue to plodding moral essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in satiric exposure of vices
rubrics_metrics.description: "He would not quite the women's frailty bare, But stript them to the waist, and left them there."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be judicious: over-exposing or mercilessly stripping a class or sex of all protection can be crude or offensive. Leave some restraint or humanity in portrayals rather than gratuitous debasement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absurd or vulgar scenes that jar taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'absurd and vulgar scene, in which the prince pretends a fit of the cholic,' likely contributed to the play's failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes that come across as inelegant, absurdly staged, or vulgarly farcical can alienate audiences and undermine a play's reputation; theatrical tricks should suit the tone and intelligence of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality resides in treatment, not subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "Originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A familiar plot or stock subject can be original if handled with new perspective, voice, or technique. Critics value novel treatment over merely novel material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and actors' quality determine reception
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poet and performers are nearly equally involved in the disgrace of a condemned piece"; players' shame and acting matter to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-written plays can fail through poor acting or staging; casting, delivery, and production quality are crucial to how audiences receive a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience caprice and preconceptions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectators 'who, perhaps, could at the very time have given no good reason for their capricious condemnation'; enemies 'resolved to damn it for the title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public taste can be fickle and prejudiced; hostile preconceptions, organized opposition, or a capricious crowd can doom a play regardless of intrinsic merit. Anticipate and, where possible, manage audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive shocking or blood‑soaked additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some practitioners ('stabbing wits') would augment plays with murders, rapes, and parricides; such brutality is criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overloading a play with sensational or gruesome material for shock value can be poor taste and provoke censure; maintain proportionality between tone and violent content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful adaptation / avoid mangling translations and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ravenscroft 'translated and mangled several' French comedies and was charged with appropriating material; Langbaine and others attacked such plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptations should be skillful and honest; crude or opportunistic translations that simply appropriate foreign material invite literary criticism and can damage reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inelegant theatrical devices (bad 'jeu de theatre')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'inelegant jeu de theatre' (e.g., the feigned fit of cholic) is subject to ridicule in satires like the 'Rehearsal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrived stage tricks and clumsy business that serve only to elicit cheap laughs are likely to be mocked and can lower a play's standing; prefer theatrical devices that emerge naturally from character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relatable examples to engage and satirize your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "By examples drawn, I dare to say, From most of you who hear and see the play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire that draws on audience-recognizable foibles and local manners fosters identification and sharper effect; grounding attacks in familiar examples increases impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-awareness and tempering of the author's satire
rubrics_metrics.description: "The men's faults are less severely shown, For he considers that himself is one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirist's awareness of his own fallibility or complicity softens harshness and can make critique more tolerable and persuasive; outright hypocrisy weakens moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public polemics and pre-performance rhetoric shape reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacks and counter-attacks in prologues, epilogues, and rival authorship (e.g., prologues attacking Dryden) affected public response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rhetorical framing around a production—prologues, dedications, public quarrels—can inflame or predispose audiences; manage public discourse and anticipate rivals' attacks.
